name: Old App Versions and API Compatibility
intent: Keep every server change working for the app versions already installed: change the API only by adding, never remove or repurpose a field, tolerate unknown fields on both sides, let the server see the client's version, and keep a forced upgrade as the last resort.
scenario: A shopping app releases v4 on day 0. Before that, 10% of users were on v1, 20% on v2 and 70% on v3. About 8% never update, and the rest adopt v4 along a slowing curve: 68.5% are on v4 after 14 days. The backend renames a field on day 14, which every client before v4 still reads under its old name: 314,414 of 1,000,000 active users break. Adding a field instead breaks 26,401, and adapting to the version header breaks none.
problem: A web page is updated for everyone the moment you deploy. An installed app is not: users update when they want, some never do, and app stores add a review delay to every release. For weeks or months several versions run side by side and all of them call your API. A change that is safe for the newest app, such as renaming a field or removing an endpoint, crashes or silently misbehaves for everyone who has not updated, and you cannot roll that back by redeploying the client.

howItWorks.title: Measure which versions are in use
howItWorks.text: Have the app send its version and platform on every request, usually in a header. Log it, and count active users per version. That count is the real compatibility requirement: you must support every version that still has users, and you can see how fast the old ones fade. Expect a long tail and a share that never updates.

howItWorks.title: Change the API by adding
howItWorks.text: Add new fields and new endpoints and leave the old ones working. Never remove a field, rename it, change its type or give it a new meaning. To rename, add the new name and keep sending the old one until the old versions are gone. Clients should ignore fields they do not know and use safe defaults for fields that are missing, so the server can add, and the client can run against a server it has never seen.

howItWorks.title: Let the server adapt to the client
howItWorks.text: Because the server knows each client's version, it can send each one the shape it understands: translate new data to the old format for old clients, or serve different behaviour per version. This keeps the new API clean while old apps keep working. Feature flags on the server can switch a behaviour on for new versions and off for old ones without a release.

howItWorks.title: Set a minimum version, and a way to retire
howItWorks.text: When an old version becomes too costly to support, or has a security problem, raise a minimum supported version. A client below it shows an update screen, a forced upgrade, instead of calling the API. It is a last resort: it blocks users until they update and some may leave, so announce it early, show a soft nudge first and keep the screen to a message and a store link.

howItWorks.title: Remove old behaviour only when few users remain
howItWorks.text: Decide to drop an old field or endpoint from data: the share of active users on versions that need it, and whether the remaining ones can be moved by a forced upgrade. Waiting for 90% adoption is not enough: 10% of a large user base is still a lot of people. Expect to keep old behaviour for months, or to accept a planned forced upgrade.

pros: Releasing a backend change never breaks users who have not updated
The server can change faster than the apps, since compatibility is a rule and not a coordination meeting
Version data tells you when an old behaviour is safe to remove
A minimum version and a kill switch give you a way out of a broken or insecure release
cons: The API accumulates old fields and code paths, so it gets harder to understand and test
Every change needs a compatibility check against all live versions, not just the newest
Adapting per version adds branches on the server that someone has to remember to delete
A forced upgrade costs users: some give up on the app instead of updating
whenToUse: Any backend serving native mobile apps, desktop apps or devices that the user updates on their own schedule
APIs used by partners, where you cannot force a new version
Rollouts of a new API where old and new clients must work against the same servers
whenNotToUse: A web front end that ships together with its backend and is always the latest version, where plain versioned deployments are enough
Keeping every version of every endpoint for ever: set a support policy and retire versions
Using a forced upgrade as the normal way to ship a change, instead of a rare safety measure
pitfalls: Renaming or removing a field because the new app no longer uses it
Clients that fail on an unknown field or a missing optional field, so even an additive change breaks them
Not sending the app version, so the server cannot tell who it is talking to
Judging safety by the newest version's adoption, and ignoring the long tail of old versions and the users who never update
Forcing an upgrade without warning or a store link, locking people out of the app
Leaving per-version workarounds in the server for years after the last user of that version is gone

roles.label: User
roles.description: Updates the app when they choose to, or never.

roles.label: Installed app
roles.description: One of several versions in use at once; sends its version with each request.

roles.label: API server
roles.description: Serves every live version and can adapt its answer to the client's version.

roles.label: App store
roles.description: Delivers new versions after review; the team cannot update users itself.

roles.label: Backend team
roles.description: Ships server changes and decides when old behaviour can go.

quiz.question: The backend team renames the field 'total' to 'amount_due' in every response, and the new app version reads 'amount_due'. Three weeks after the release, 70% of users are on the new version. What happens?
options: The 30% on older versions break, because they still read 'total' and the field is gone.
Nothing breaks, because most users have moved to the new version.
The older versions switch to the new name automatically when they see a new response.
Only the oldest version breaks, because newer ones ignore unknown fields.
quiz.explanation: A rename removes the old name for clients that have not updated. Adoption of the new version is irrelevant for the others. Safe rename: send both fields until the versions that read 'total' are gone.

quiz.question: Which server change is safe for an old app that ignores fields it does not recognise?
options: Changing 'price' from a number of cents to a string with a currency symbol.
Adding an optional 'discount_label' field to each item.
Reusing an old 'status' code for a new meaning.
Removing the 'avatar_url' field, since the new app does not need it.
quiz.explanation: Adding an optional field is the compatible change: old clients that ignore unknown fields never see a difference. Changing a type, repurposing a value or removing a field all alter something the old client depends on.

quiz.question: A security bug is found in app v2, which 5% of users still run. The server can no longer protect them. What is the right tool?
options: Ship a fix for the server only; apps do not matter.
Rename the API fields so that v2 stops working.
Raise the minimum supported version, so that v2 shows an update screen.
Wait until adoption of the new version reaches 100%.
quiz.explanation: A forced upgrade is the designed last resort for a version that must no longer be used. Breaking it by accident with a rename gives users no explanation. Waiting is not an option, as some users never update.
